title: From Ancient China to NASA: The Surprising Science of Paper Airplanes
summary:
What do ancient Chinese inventors, Japanese origami masters, and NASA engineers have in common? They all helped shape the humble paper airplane. May 26 marks National Paper Airplane Day, a celebration of the folded flyer that has captivated kids and adults for generations. But this simple toy has a surprisingly rich history and some serious science behind it. 

The practice of folding paper into gliders likely began in ancient China, where paper was invented around 105 CE. The art was later refined in Japan, where it became known as aerogami—a blend of origami and aeronautics. In the United States, the first known instructions for a "paper dart" appeared in an 1859 children's book, meaning people have been folding these flyers for over 167 years. The term "paper airplane" wasn't coined until 1907, and it overtook "paper dart" as the popular name by the 1950s. 

If you think your paper airplane skills are impressive, consider the world records. In 2022, Kim Kyu Tae hurled a paper plane an astonishing 252.6 feet—that's longer than the wingspan of a Boeing 737. The record for longest flight duration is 31.2 seconds, achieved by a team in China. Both feats required not just a strong throw, but careful design and precise folding. 

Want to fold like a pro? NASA, the agency known for moon landings and Mars rovers, has you covered. The first "A" in NASA stands for aeronautics, and the agency offers free, step-by-step tutorials for crafting paper versions of its experimental aircraft. You can build a colorful generic plane, or tackle models of the X-57 Maxwell (an all-electric research plane) and the X-59 Quiet SuperSonic Technology aircraft, designed to reduce sonic booms. These designs let you explore the same principles of lift, drag, and thrust that real engineers use. 

So this National Paper Airplane Day, grab a sheet of paper and start folding. Whether you're aiming for distance, hang time, or just a cool design, you're part of a centuries-old tradition that connects art, history, and cutting-edge science.

background_read: Paper was invented in China around 105 CE by Cai Lun, a court official, and paper folding soon became a popular pastime. In Japan, the art of origami ('folding paper') developed into a highly refined practice.

By the 19th century, folded paper darts appeared in English children's literature: 'The Boy's Own Toy-maker' (1859) by Ebenezer Landells included instructions for a 'paper dart', marking the earliest known printed guide. The modern term 'paper airplane' only gained popularity in the 1900s.

Today, enthusiasts like Kim Kyu Tae (a South Korean who set the distance world record of 252.6 feet in 2022) and teams in China push the limits of design. NASA's aeronautics branch, which studies flight within Earth's atmosphere, provides online tutorials for paper versions of experimental aircraft such as the X-57 Maxwell (an all-electric plane) and the X-59 (designed to reduce sonic booms).

perspectives.description: Paper airplanes are a fun, low-cost way to explore physics and creativity; NASA's involvement shows they can lead to real engineering interest.
Some see them as just toys, overlooking the serious scientific concepts they can teach, and may dismiss them as childish without understanding their depth.
The long history across cultures illustrates how simple technologies evolve, spread, and merge—folding art meets experimental flight—over centuries.
As aviation seeks quieter, greener designs, the foundational ideas explored through paper airplanes could inspire the next generation of aircraft engineers.
